sections.h2: How does probate work in Illinois?
sections.html:
Probate is the court process that settles a dead person's affairs: a personal representative gathers the property, pays valid debts and expenses, and gives what is left to the people entitled to it. With a valid will the estate is distributed under the will, and without one Illinois inheritance law decides who receives what. A person named in the will is called the executor, and a court-appointed representative when there is no will is called the administrator.

A case opens in the circuit court of the county where the decedent lived. Illinois Legal Aid Online says an Illinois-licensed lawyer must file the case, because the estate is a separate legal entity that cannot represent itself, and that a family member who tries to file alone will be told to hire a lawyer.

sections.h2: When does a house have to go through probate?
sections.html:
Probate is usually needed when the person owned real estate in their name alone and nothing moves it automatically at death. A house held in joint tenancy with survivorship, held in a trust, or covered by a recorded Transfer on Death Instrument passes outside probate. A will alone does not avoid probate, because the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

For a surviving spouse, a jointly owned home normally becomes the survivor's property. If the house was only in the deceased spouse's name, probate may still be needed. The title company decides what it needs to insure a sale, so ask it early which documents it will accept.

  • Sole name, no beneficiary designation: probate is usually required.
  • Joint tenancy with survivorship: passes to the surviving owner.
  • Trust or Transfer on Death Instrument: follows the instrument.

sections.h2: What are the steps from filing to closing the estate?
sections.html:
The lawyer files a petition in the right county. With a will, the petition asks the court to admit it and name the executor, and the court will not look at the petition until the will itself is on file. The law requires whoever holds a will to file it with the clerk right after death. Once the court is satisfied, it appoints the representative and issues letters of office.

Then come notices to creditors, collecting and protecting the property, paying debts and expenses, and distribution. Illinois does not use one statewide form set, so the circuit clerk of the county supplies the petitions and notices.

Core Illinois probate rules that affect a house sale. Source: 755 ILCS 5 on ilga.gov and Illinois Legal Aid Online.

Independent administrationRepresentative acts without court orders unless the Article or an interested person requires them5/28-1

Under Article 28 an executor or administrator can administer the estate without a court order or filings, except where the Article or an interested person asks for court involvement. An independent representative who acts reasonably for the estate's best interests may lease, mortgage, or sell the decedent's real estate at public or private sale, for cash or on credit, without asking the judge.

One limit matters for a sale: real estate that the will specifically leaves to a named person cannot be leased, sold or mortgaged without that person's written consent. A representative can also confirm title in an heir or legatee by recording an instrument that releases the estate's interest.

Any interested person can petition to end independent status. The court must grant it unless the will directs independent administration, in which case it needs good cause, or the petitioner is a creditor or a legatee other than a residuary legatee, in which case it must find that termination is necessary to protect that person. After termination, the representative follows the rules for supervised administration.

sections.h2: How do creditor claims affect the timing of a sale?
sections.html:
Creditors have a set window to file. The published notice states a claim date no earlier than six months after the first publication or three months after the notice is mailed or delivered, whichever is later. A claim not filed by that date is barred, and in any event claims are barred two years after death.

A representative who gives proper notice in good faith is not personally liable to a creditor, but a claim that is not barred can still be pursued against assets that have not been distributed and against a distributee, up to the amount the distributee received above what they would have gotten had the claim been paid. The bar does not cut off actions to establish the decedent's liability to the extent liability insurance covers it.

sections.h2: What happens if there is no will?
sections.html:
A person who dies without a valid will is intestate, and Illinois law picks the heirs. Property may go to a surviving spouse, children, parents or other relatives as the statute sets out, which can differ from what the person would have chosen. The court names an administrator, who has the same duties as an executor: collect assets, pay debts and expenses, and distribute the rest.

If you find a will after the case starts, take it to the lawyer at once and file it with the clerk. The Probate Act makes it a Class 3 felony to willfully alter or destroy a will without the testator's direction, or to hide one for 30 days after learning of the death.

  • Locate the original will, not a copy.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it wants, since title companies often need to see the letters of office.
  • Keep a list of every parcel the decedent owned, because each deed may need its own recording.

sections.h2: Can a small estate skip probate?
sections.html:
Some can, but not when a house is involved. Illinois Legal Aid Online says a small estate affidavit may be used only if the estate has no real estate, at least 60 days have passed since the death, no probate petition is filed or pending, and total personal property is $150,000 or less. Registered motor vehicles are listed on the affidavit but do not count toward the cap.

The statute, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, also requires that the affiant pay valid claims before distributing to heirs. The affidavit transfers personal property such as accounts, not land. A homeowner heir should plan for either a probate case, a trust, a Transfer on Death Instrument, or joint title to move a house.

  • Check how the deed reads before assuming probate is needed.
  • Ask the circuit clerk in the county of death for forms and local steps.
  • Illinois Legal Aid Online lists a free application for people who cannot afford a lawyer.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to open probate in Illinois?
faqs.a: Yes. Illinois Legal Aid Online says an Illinois-licensed lawyer must open the case, and the court will pause a case filed by a family member until counsel is found.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell the house during probate?
faqs.a: Often yes. An independent representative may sell real estate without a court order under 755 ILCS 5/28-8, but property specifically left to a legatee needs that person's written consent.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims?
faqs.a: The notice sets a date at least six months after first publication or three months after mailing, whichever is later. All claims are barred two years after death regardless of letters (755 ILCS 5/18-3 and 18-12).

faqs.q: Does a will avoid probate in Illinois?
faqs.a: No. A will names who gets the property and often names the executor, but if the property must pass through probate the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

faqs.q: Which court handles an Illinois probate case?
faqs.a: The circuit court in the county where the decedent lived. Forms and filing steps differ by county, so the circuit clerk's office or website is where to look.
